title: Hardware operational lifetime failure between interval bounds
scenario_markdown: The operational lifetime $X$ (in operating hours) of an electric vehicle power inverter module follows an exponential distribution with a mean lifetime of $\mu = 1{,}000$ operating hours (failure rate $\lambda = 1/1{,}000 = 0.001\text{ hr}^{-1}$). Reliability engineers need to determine the probability that a module fails between 500 and 1,500 operating hours ($P(500 < X < 1{,}500)$).
assumptions: Mean time between failures mu = 1,000 hours
Single point mass probabilities are zero (P(X = c) = 0)

stages.prompt_markdown: How is the probability of failing between 500 and 1,500 hours, $P(500 < X < 1500)$, expressed in terms of the exponential cumulative distribution function $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$?

options.hint_markdown: Cumulative probabilities overlap; subtracting $F(500)$ from $F(1500)$ strips out the lower tail up to 500.
The exponential distribution has a decaying density, not a uniform constant density.

stages.explanation_markdown: The probability of an interval $[x_1, x_2]$ is the difference between cumulative distribution function values: $P(x_1 < X < x_2) = F(x_2) - F(x_1) = (1 - e^{-\lambda x_2}) - (1 - e^{-\lambda x_1}) = e^{-\lambda x_1} - e^{-\lambda x_2} = e^{-0.5} - e^{-1.5}$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate $P(500 < X < 1500) = e^{-0.5} - e^{-1.5}$. Enter as a decimal rounded to at least three places (e.g., 0.383 or 0.3834).
For this continuous exponential distribution, how does the strict inequality probability $P(500 < X < 1500)$ compare to the non-strict inequality probability $P(500 \le X \le 1500)$?

options.text_markdown: They are strictly equal ($P(500 < X < 1500) = P(500 \le X \le 1500)$) because the probability of continuous $X$ taking any exact single value is zero ($P(X = 500) = 0$ and $P(X = 1500) = 0$)
The non-strict probability is strictly larger because it includes point masses at 500 and 1500
options.hint_markdown: In continuous distributions, the area under the curve at a single point is zero width, so boundary points contribute zero probability.

options.text_markdown: In Excel, one must evaluate `=EXPON.DIST(1499.9, ...)` to reflect strict inequality
options.hint_markdown: Continuous variables do not require endpoint subtraction or adjustment; $F(x)$ is continuous everywhere for $x > 0$.

stages.explanation_markdown: In continuous probability models, $P(X = c) = \int_c^c f(x)\,dx = 0$ for any real number $c$. Therefore: $P(a < X < b) = P(a \le X < b) = P(a < X \le b) = P(a \le X \le b)$. Whether the endpoints are included makes no difference to the probability.
